samples.text:
The pie charts shows how the students of a college went to the campus in 2000 and 2020.

In 2000, car was the most popular way to travel, with 46% of students. Bus was second with 30%. Walking was 12%, bicycle was 8% and train was the lowest with only 4%. So most of students used a car or a bus at that time.

In 2020, there were many changes. The number of students who used car fell down to 21%, which is less than the half of 2000. Bus stayed nearly same at 28% and it became the most popular way. On the other hand, the bicycle increased very much from 8% to 25%. Walking also increased a little to 15% and train went up to 11%.

To sum up, the car was the main transport in 2000 but in 2020 students used more bus and bicycle. Using the train and walking also became more popular, so the students used more different ways to get to the college than before.
samples.why: Main changes identified with accurate figures · overview only in the final paragraph · simple, repetitive linking · adequate vocabulary with some imprecision (number/percentage) · several article and agreement errors.

samples.text:
The pie charts illustrate the modes of transport that students at a college used to get to campus in 2000 and 2020.

Overall, the car lost its position as the dominant form of transport over the twenty-year period, while cycling became far more popular. By 2020, the bus was the most common way of travelling to college.

In 2000, almost half of all students (46%) drove to campus, and a further 30% took the bus. Only a small minority walked (12%) or cycled (8%), and the train was the least popular option, used by just 4% of students.

Twenty years later, the proportion of students travelling by car had fallen by more than half, to 21%. The bus remained relatively stable at 28%, which meant that it overtook the car as the most frequently used mode. The most dramatic change was in cycling, which rose from 8% to 25%, more than tripling. The figures for walking and the train also increased, to 15% and 11% respectively, indicating that students were using a wider range of transport than before.
samples.why: Clear overview of the main shifts · key features well selected and supported with accurate figures · logical progression · varied cohesive devices · good vocabulary with few errors.

samples.text:
The two charts compare the ways in which students at a college travelled to campus in 2000 and 2020.

The overriding trend is a marked shift away from the car towards more sustainable modes of transport, particularly cycling. As a result, students' choices were considerably more balanced in 2020 than they had been two decades earlier.

In 2000, the car was clearly the preferred option, accounting for 46% of journeys, and when combined with the bus (30%) it covered more than three-quarters of all trips to campus. Walking and cycling were relatively uncommon, at 12% and 8% respectively, and only 4% of students commuted by train.

By 2020, reliance on the car had diminished substantially, with its share falling to 21%, so that the bus, despite a slight dip to 28%, became the leading mode. The most remarkable growth occurred in cycling, which more than tripled to 25% and thus overtook both walking and the car. Rail travel also gained ground, almost trebling from 4% to 11%, while walking increased modestly to 15%. Consequently, no single mode of transport accounted for even a third of journeys by the end of the period.
samples.why: Key features skilfully selected with a well-placed overview · accurate, comparative use of figures (more than tripled, almost trebling) · cohesion well managed · precise vocabulary · wide range of error-free structures.
